content:
Hewlett Packard Enterprise announced Oct. 20 that its fourth-generation Spaceborne Computer will fly to the Moon to run artificial intelligence and the first high-performance computing benchmarks ever attempted on the lunar surface.

The module, HPE Spaceborne Computer-4, is a compact unit — roughly 249 by 132 by 26 millimeters in an aluminum chassis, loaded with KIOXIA solid-state drives — built to survive space's radiation, temperature swings and power constraints. It will ride as a payload on Astrolab's FLIP (Flex Lunar Innovation Platform) rover, which Voyager Technologies' Griffin-1 lander is scheduled to deliver near the Moon's south pole. The mission is targeting launch in late 2026 as part of NASA's Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) program, which buys rides to the Moon from commercial vendors.

Three AI workloads are planned for the lunar surface: large-language-model retrieval-augmented generation, vision inference, and LiDAR data processing for terrain analysis and navigation mapping. NASA will also run its FLUID federated-learning experiment — training a neural network across data from Earth, the Moon and the International Space Station — plus a test of a tuned language model for searching and interpreting onboard documents. Deloitte plans to deploy Silent Shield, a cyber intrusion-detection system, on the same mission.

The logic is practical: with communications delays between Earth and the Moon, tight power budgets and a harsh environment, processing data where it is collected matters more than beaming it all home. "The next chapter of lunar exploration will depend on the ability to turn data into insights at the point of discovery," said Scott Wiest, HPE vice president, fellow and global sales chief technologist. Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews called the Moon "a challenging environment for advanced computing" and said the mission will show how commercial rovers can carry research payloads.

The mission extends HPE's Spaceborne Computer program, which previously flew experiments aboard the International Space Station, from low-Earth orbit to the lunar surface — a proving ground for the computing infrastructure a sustained Moon presence, and eventually Mars missions, will require.

Sources: HPE press release (Oct. 20, 2026); BusinessWire.

— Walter Webb & Willa Webb, News Anchors, Webb Watch 956

title: A Houston-built computer is headed to the Moon to run AI on the lunar surface
